key_claims: A four-month supervised exercise and education program improved knee pain, muscle strength, and quality of life in young adults with persistent symptoms following ACL reconstruction.
The supervised rehabilitation intervention showed no evidence of damaging knee cartilage or worsening early-stage knee osteoarthritis.
The SUPER-Knee trial evaluated an intervention targeting adults aged 18 to 40 who continued to experience knee symptoms one to three years post-surgery.
The exercise program relies on low resource needs and does not require specialized equipment or extra staff training.
limitations: The trial did not establish whether the program prevents long-term knee osteoarthritis.
The study specifically focused on young adults aged 18 to 40 with persistent symptoms after ACL reconstruction, limiting immediate applicability to other populations.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that the exercise program definitively prevents knee osteoarthritis in the long term.
Do not state that physical therapy guarantees a full return to contact sports or complete pain elimination for all patients.
Do not extrapolate the results to older adults or individuals who did not undergo ACL reconstruction.
